title: The Roundup
subtitle: Monday 10 to Saturday 22 May 1886: Mavericks, a Survey Stake at the Narrows, a Blizzard's Tail and Fire on the Flats

setting.name: The Sage Flats roundup and the survey camp, May 1886
setting.description: Every May the Platte River Stock Growers' Association holds the general spring roundup: every outfit on the range sends its wagon, its riders and its 'reps', and for two weeks they sweep the country together, gather every cow, cut each outfit's cattle out of the herd and brand the calves, each calf to the brand its mother wears. The motherless, unbranded calves, mavericks, go by Association rule to the Association, which means to the big outfits. This year the Bitter Creek roundup works out of the Sage Flats below the Narrows, with the Company's two wagons, sixty riders and a remuda of five hundred horses, and the grange's own wagon with a dozen homesteaders and small ranchers repping for their few hundred head. Wade Tolliver is roundup boss. Jubal Stroud and the Association gunmen ride with the Company 'to watch for rustling'. On 12 May the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway's survey party comes down out of the foothills and pitches its tents a mile off, and begins driving stakes up the creek toward the Narrows. On the night of 15 May, the tail of a late blizzard comes down the valley. The roundup is a moving town of men and cattle, a pressure cooker of armed rivals working side by side, and the best place in the territory to find out things.
setting.atmosphere: Dust, bawling, smoke and the smell of burning hair from the branding fires. The Sage Flats are going green and the sky is huge and blue and then, on the 15th, iron grey. Thousands of cattle, longhorn crosses and shorthorn bulls, mill in the day herd; riders cut and rope at a gallop; the cook's triangle rings at four in the morning; men sleep in their bedrolls by the wagons and night guard sings to the herd. The work is dangerous and skilled and the men are proud of it. Everyone is armed. The grange's wagon is camped a quarter mile from the Company's, and the space between them is a border. Then the snow: a wall of white coming down the valley in the afternoon, the temperature falling forty degrees in an hour, the herd drifting with the wind, and a night of howling dark when a stampede is one thunderclap away.

keyLocations.name: The roundup camp on the Sage Flats
keyLocations.description: Two Company chuck wagons and a bed wagon, the grange's single wagon a quarter mile off, a rope corral for the remuda, the day herd of three thousand head held on the flats by circling riders, and the branding fires where the calves are roped, dragged, thrown and branded. Tolliver runs it from horseback. Every evening the reps argue over the day's mavericks around the fire.
features: The branding fires and the tally book, where the Company's tally man records each calf's brand; the grange's rep keeps a tally of his own and they never agree
The cut: riders separating each outfit's cattle from the herd, the most skilled riding on the range and the most dangerous place to start a quarrel
The night guard, two riders at a time circling the herd and singing
The Company's camp, with Stroud's grey horse tied apart from the others
encounters: Mavericks: a branding-fire quarrel between the Company's tally man and the grange's rep over calves following homesteaders' cows
A Longhorn Bull that does not want to be cut
Ira Pettit and Elam Henley, hired on as day riders for the grange's wagon (Sayre found them the work)
secrets: CLUE B4 (core for anyone who spends an evening near Ira Pettit, especially a Preacher or anyone kind): Pettit is drinking from a bottle he hides in his bedroll, and on the second night, by the grange wagon's fire, he says to nobody in particular, 'It takes so long. Nobody tells you it takes so long.' Then he sees Henley watching him and stops.

Insight DC 14 on Pettit: he wants to confess. He is more afraid of Henley than of the law. If the party gets him alone and promises him protection and a trial, not a rope, he tells them everything (CLUE B6 and C6): the $100 each, the $200 more promised, the notary's office on the Friday night, Sayre lettering the sign at his desk 'like he was writing a birthday card', and the relinquishment they signed as witnesses on the Saturday.

Henley knows Pettit is coming apart. On the night of the blizzard (15 May), unless Pettit is with the party or under guard, Henley takes him out to the herd 'to help with night guard', shoots him in the dark when the storm is loudest, and leaves the body where the stampede will go over it. The cattle do the rest.

The Company's tally man, a clerk from Laramie, has orders from Ballantine to tally every unbranded calf as a maverick for the Association, including calves following grange cows, and to tally grange strays with brands 'not on the Association's book' as mavericks too. The grange's twelve homesteaders lose about forty calves this way unless someone stops it.

keyLocations.name: The survey camp
keyLocations.description: A mile up the flats from the roundup: four wall tents, a cook tent, a wagon of stakes and chain, the instrument tent with its transit, level and drawing table, and nine men of the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway's location survey under chief engineer Horace Wendt. From 12 May they drive a line of numbered stakes up the creek toward the Narrows, a few miles a day. The survey party is neutral, busy and hungry for beef, and it brought the winter's records with it.
features: The drawing table and the profile: a long roll of paper showing the line's grades up the valley, with a dam, a water tank and a 'Div. Pt.' at the Narrows
The paymaster's tin box with the survey party's payroll book and the time book, kept by Wendt himself
The line of stakes, painted red and numbered, marching up the creek
Henry Lau's instrument, a brass transit, and his notebooks
encounters: Chief engineer Horace Wendt, gruff and kind, who liked Owen Lasker
Henry Lau, the instrument man (companion), who knew Owen all winter
Company riders who come by to tell the surveyors that the Company owns the creek and to ask where the line is going
secrets: CLUE C2 (core for anyone who asks Wendt or Henry Lau about Owen's work over the winter, or reads the payroll book): Owen Lasker was on the survey party's payroll as chainman from January to 13 April; the time book shows him in the foothill camp, forty miles from Gilead, every day from 6 to 13 April, including 10 April, the date of the relinquishment Sayre holds. He could not have signed it in Gilead that day. Wendt will lend the book, or swear to it before a judge.

CLUE E1 (core for anyone shown the profile; Wendt will not show it to Company men, and Henry Lau will show it to friends): the railroad's water station, a dam to hold water for the engines, and a division point with a roundhouse and townsite are planned at the Narrows. Whoever owns the Narrows quarter can sell it to the railroad for thousands. Wendt: 'Owen copied that sheet for me in March. Asked a lot of questions.'

Wendt has received a letter, forwarded from the railroad's land department in Omaha, saying that 'a local party, Mr. G. Sayre, U.S. Commissioner, has offered the Narrows quarter with title to be clear by June' and asking Wendt's opinion of the site. He thinks nothing of it unless asked. If asked who had offered the Narrows, he remembers the name. (A first glimpse of CLUE C5.)

Wendt also has Owen's last letter to him, the fair copy of the draft in the coffee can (CLUE E2): Owen offered to sell the Narrows to the railroad on condition the dam leave water for the ditches below. Wendt was going to recommend it.

keyLocations.name: The Company's hay camp
keyLocations.description: Two miles up the flats from the roundup, on the creek: a line-camp cabin, corrals, and twelve long stacks of last summer's wild hay, the Company's winter feed for its saddle horses and weak cattle, worth $3,000 and a great deal more in a bad winter. Two riders keep it.
features: Twelve haystacks, each the size of a house, dry as tinder on top
The line cabin with a sheet-iron stove, two bunks and a Company rifle
The creek bank, where riders can come up unseen from the willows
encounters: Nils Solberg and four young homesteaders (use Rustler), with lanterns and coal oil, on the night of 17 May
Two Company line riders (use Hired Gun at the GM's discretion, or Drunk Cowboy if they have been at the roundup whiskey)
secrets: After the ambush on Calvin Booker's rider on 13 May, Nils Solberg decides to burn the Company's hay. If he does, the Company counts it as the grange's 'outrage in kind', which is what Ballantine needs to justify the raid, and in the winter to come those stacks would have been the difference between life and death for six hundred cattle.
Gideon Sayre suggested the hay to Nils, in passing, at a grange meeting in early May: 'Hay is the one thing a cattle company cannot buy in February.'

keyLocations.name: The Forks: Ballantine's office
keyLocations.description: The BC Home Ranch, emptied for the roundup: a skeleton crew, the cook, Ballantine and his Scots clerk. Ballantine rides down to the roundup most days and back at night.
features: Ballantine's desk, his letter book and the telegraph-form pad, on which the top sheet carries the impression of the last message
A locked tin box of Association correspondence
encounters: Cyrus Ballantine
Duncan Lyall, the Company's clerk, who is honest and frightened
secrets: CLUE D3 (Investigation DC 12 on the telegraph pad's impression, or Persuasion DC 15 on Lyall, who copied it out): 'WILL CLEAR CREEK AFTER ROUNDUP STOP NEED PAPERS FROM RAWLINS FOR NINE NAMES STOP SEND FUNDS STOP BALLANTINE.' Sent 14 May by rider to Rawlins.

The tin box holds the Association's annotated copy of the dead list, with 'per G.S., Gilead' beside six names (CLUE C3). Mechanics DC 15 to open it. Ballantine does not know who G.S. is and has never cared. A party that gets it now has the campaign's strongest single clue a scenario early; let them.

keyLocations.name: Booker's Draw
keyLocations.description: A side valley south of the creek, two miles long, with a spring at its head, Calvin Booker's log house, horse corrals, and a hundred head of cattle under his Lazy CB brand. Booker and his rider, Joe Pruneda, a Tejano horse-breaker from San Antonio, are repping for the grange at the roundup, and ride home to see to the place every other night.
features: The narrow mouth of the draw between two cedar-grown ridges, the only way in for a wagon
The spring and the stone springhouse
The four nail holes on Booker's door where Stroud's thirty-day card went up on 17 April; Booker carries the card. Its thirty days run out on 17 May, and Stroud is waiting for the warrants of the 24th
encounters: The ambush of 13 May: Stroud and two Association gunmen on the ridge above the mouth of the draw
secrets: On 13 May at dusk, Stroud and two Association gunmen wait on the cedar ridge above the mouth of the draw for Calvin Booker. Joe Pruneda rides in alone on Booker's horse, and is shot through the shoulder from three hundred yards. Stroud, seeing his mistake through the field glasses, does not fire again: Pruneda's name is on the list, but his thirty days have not run. That restraint, if the party learns of it, says everything about Stroud.

If the party is with Booker or Pruneda that evening, the ambush is a running fight at long range in failing light: Stroud's Buffalo rifle against whatever the party has. Stroud withdraws rather than fight at close range in the dark, which he considers unprofessional.

synopsis: Two weeks of the spring roundup on the Sage Flats, with the whole valley armed and working side by side. The Company tallies every doubtful calf to itself; the grange's wagon fights for every one; Stroud and the Association gunmen ride with the Company to 'watch for rustling'; and on 13 May Stroud's men shoot Calvin Booker's rider from ambush. On 12 May the railroad's survey party arrives, and its records hold the two things the party most needs: the payroll book that proves Owen Lasker was forty miles away on the day his 'relinquishment' was signed, and the profile that shows why the Narrows is worth killing for. Ira Pettit, hired on with Henley as a day rider for the grange, is coming apart and wants to confess. On the night of 15 May the tail of a spring blizzard roars down the valley, the herd stampedes, and Henley means to kill Pettit in the dark. If the party protects Pettit, they have a living witness to the hanging and to who paid for it. In the week after, Nils Solberg plans to burn the Company's hay, Ballantine wires Rawlins that he will 'clear the creek after the roundup', and Wade Tolliver, the roundup boss, sick of what his Company has become, can be turned. By the end of the roundup, the party should know that Gideon Sayre paid for the hanging and why, and should know that the Company is coming for the dead-list men when the thirty days run out on 24 May.
hook: Monday 10 May, before dawn: the cook's triangle rings on the Sage Flats, sixty riders roll out of their blankets in the frost, and Wade Tolliver, roundup boss, sitting a big dun horse with his breath smoking, reads out the day's circle. The party is here as reps, riders, guards, inspectors or just watchers, for whoever is paying them. Across the flats a mile off, a line of white tents has appeared overnight with a flag on a pole, and a man is looking through a brass instrument on three legs, straight up the valley at the Narrows.

conclusions.conclusion: C. Gideon Sayre paid for the hanging
clues: C1: the handwriting and the Land Office paper (Gilead, compared at leisure)
C2: the survey payroll proves the relinquishment a forgery (the survey camp)
C4: Owen's page, 'G.S. is the one giving names' (Thea, at the grange wagon or the Narrows)
C6: Pettit's confession that 'the notary' paid them (the roundup, if he lives)
C3: the annotated dead list, 'per G.S.' (Ballantine's tin box, if the party looks early)

conclusions.conclusion: E. The Narrows is the prize
clues: E1: the survey profile with the water station and division point (the survey camp)
E2: Owen's letter to Wendt (the survey camp, or the coffee can)
Wendt's letter from Omaha naming Sayre as offering the quarter (the survey camp)

conclusions.conclusion: D. The Company will raid the dead-list men when the thirty days run out
clues: D3: Ballantine's telegram, 'will clear creek after roundup' (the Forks)
D4: Tolliver's word, if turned (Tolliver's fire)
The Association gunmen's talk of 'papers from Rawlins' (the roundup)
The ambush at Booker's Draw and Stroud's cards, all due on 24 May (Booker's Draw)

acts.title: The General Roundup
acts.description: The first days of the roundup, 10 to 13 May: the work, the skill, the danger and the quarrels. This act is the campaign's big set piece of cowboy life, and the GM should make the work vivid: the circle at dawn, the cut, the roping, the branding fires, the night guard. Whatever side the party is on, they are riding beside the other side, eating its beef, and depending on its riders when a steer goes the wrong way. The tensions are mavericks, Stroud's presence, and Pettit's conscience. On the 13th, the ambush at Booker's Draw.
objectives: Work the roundup, and earn the respect of the riders on both sides
Settle, or win, the quarrel over the mavericks
Notice Ira Pettit, and find out what is eating him
Be at Booker's Draw on 13 May, or deal with what happened there

scenes.name: The Circle
scenes.description: Dawn of 10 May. Tolliver sends the riders out in pairs on a great circle twenty miles round, to sweep every cow toward the flats. Pair the party with riders from the other side: a Company cowboy with a grange rider, Hy Tolliver with Clara Solberg, Delfina Ochoa with Calvin Booker. The circle is hard riding over broken country, with a cow in every draw and a bog in every creek bend. Use the trail and riding rules. At noon the herd comes together on the flats in a river of dust, three thousand head bawling, and the cut begins.
scenes.readAloud: The cook's triangle rings in the dark and sixty men roll out of their blankets into frost so hard the grass crunches, and stamp, and swear, and drink coffee scalding from tin cups, and go out to the rope corral where five hundred horses are milling in the starlight. Wade Tolliver sits his big dun horse by the fire with his breath smoking and reads out the circle in a flat Texas voice, two names at a time, a Company name and a grange name, and nobody argues with him. Then the sun comes up over the Sage Flats like a struck match, and sixty riders go out in every direction at a lope, and the whole valley, green and gold and twenty miles wide, is full of men and horses and the far-off bawling of cattle that do not want to be found.

skillChecks.success: You ride the circle like a top hand, bring in more cattle than your partner, and a Company cowboy says 'not bad' in front of witnesses. The riders on both sides start treating you as one of them. Reputation +1.
skillChecks.failure: Your horse goes down in a bog hole on Rattlesnake Creek; you are wet to the waist and laughed at all evening. No harm done, except to your pride and the horse's temper.

skillChecks.success: At the cut, you work a cow and her calf out of the herd cleanly, the hardest thing on the roundup, and the calf goes to the brand its mother wears. Tolliver nods.
skillChecks.failure: A Longhorn Bull takes exception to being cut, and comes out of the herd at you (use Longhorn Bull). Riders scatter. Somebody needs to rope him or shoot him, and shooting him costs his owner $40.

skillChecks.success: Out on the circle, in a cedar draw, you find a dozen grange cattle that have been held in a brush corral and their brands freshly 'worked' into the Company's Bar BC with a running iron. Someone in the Company is stealing from the homesteaders and calling them rustlers. Tolliver did not know, and is furious.
skillChecks.failure: Long hard country and no cattle in it you did not expect.

scenes.name: Mavericks
scenes.description: Evening at the branding fires. The Company's tally man, a clerk from Laramie with orders from Ballantine, is tallying every doubtful calf as a maverick for the Association. The grange's rep, Lars Engstrom, a big Swede with a temper, is tallying them as grange calves. It comes to shouting, then to hands on guns. Tolliver as roundup boss has to decide; the party can decide it for him, with evidence, with Animal Handling (a calf follows its mother), with the rules of the Association read aloud, or with the threat of force. This scene is a small model of the whole war: the law is on the Company's side, and the Company is cheating with it.
scenes.readAloud: The branding fires burn red in the dusk and the air stinks of scorched hair. A calf bawls and is let go and runs to its mother, and the tally man, a narrow young clerk in sleeve garters and a derby hat, writes in his book: 'Maverick. Association.' A big fair-bearded man in overalls, the grange's rep, puts his hand flat on the book. 'That calf sucked a Solberg cow ten minutes ago. I saw it. Everybody saw it.' The clerk does not look up. 'Unbranded calves on the open range are mavericks under the Association's rules, Mr. Engstrom, and I have my instructions.' The fire crackles. Around it, two dozen men, half from each wagon, have stopped what they were doing, and their hands are not on their ropes any more.

skillChecks.success: You prove it in front of everyone: turn the calf loose and it goes straight to the Solberg cow and sucks. Even the Company riders laugh. Tolliver rules that every calf that mothers up goes to its mother's brand, by the oldest custom on the range, and tells the tally man to write it down. The grange recovers its forty calves.
skillChecks.failure: The calf runs to the wrong cow. The tally man smirks. Engstrom reaches for his rifle.

skillChecks.success: You talk it down by talking to the riders, not the clerk: these men have worked beside each other all day and none of them wants to die over a calf. Hands come off guns. Tolliver takes the tally book away from the clerk. Grange and Company attitudes both improve by a step toward the party.
skillChecks.failure: The quarrel goes on and somebody is going to draw. Tolliver will have to stop it, and he is looking at you to see which side you are on.

skillChecks.success: One look and the clerk closes his book. It works, but it was the party's guns that settled it, not the custom, and Stroud, watching from the Company wagon, notes who you are.
skillChecks.failure: The Association gunmen drift over to stand behind the clerk. Now it is a standoff, and Stroud is smiling.

scenes.name: The Ambush at Booker's Draw
scenes.description: Thursday 13 May, dusk. Calvin Booker asks Joe Pruneda to ride home and see to the horses in Booker's Draw. Stroud and two Association gunmen are waiting on the cedar ridge above the mouth of the draw for Booker, whose thirty days have four to run; Stroud means only to watch, the Association gunmen mean more. One fires early, at Pruneda on Booker's horse. If the party rides with Pruneda, this is a long-range fight in failing light; Stroud withdraws rather than fight close in the dark. If not, Pruneda comes back to the roundup at midnight with a bullet through the shoulder, and Booker and Nils Solberg want to ride on the Company's camp. Either way, Stroud's restraint is the clue: he stopped his men firing again because Pruneda's thirty days had not run. A party that hears this from Pruneda ('the tall one knocked the other's rifle up') should begin to understand him.
scenes.readAloud: The mouth of Booker's Draw is a gap between two cedar-dark ridges with the last of the light going copper on their tops, and the spring creek talking to itself in the bottom. Joe Pruneda is singing in Spanish, something about a girl in San Antonio, and his horse's ears are up. Then a flash on the ridge, high and to the left, and the flat smack of a rifle a long heartbeat after, and Pruneda is out of the saddle and in the creek. A second flash. Then, faint and far off on the ridge against the copper sky, you see a tall figure in a grey coat reach out and knock the other rifle's barrel up toward the sky, and the shot goes off into nothing.

skillChecks.success: Three men on the ridge, three hundred yards, one of them in a grey coat on a grey horse: Stroud. He stopped the second shot. They are already leaving.
skillChecks.failure: Rifle flashes in the cedar, and then nothing. You do not know how many.

skillChecks.success: You get Pruneda out of the creek, stop the bleeding and splint the arm. He will live and ride again in a month. He says, through his teeth, 'The tall one stopped them. Why would he stop them?'
skillChecks.failure: He is bleeding badly; you need Dr. Haskell or a Doc's Sawbones within the hour, which means a hard ride to Gilead or the survey camp, where there is a medical kit.

skillChecks.success: On the ridge in the morning: three horses, the grey's long stride, brass from a Buffalo rifle and a carbine, and a cartridge-box card torn in half and dropped. It is a warning card made out to Joe Pruneda, dated 20 April. Thirty days from 20 April is 20 May. Stroud tore it up, as if he had broken his own rule and could not stand to keep the evidence.
skillChecks.failure: Tracks of three horses going north toward the Forks, and nothing else.

encounters: A Longhorn Bull at the cut
The maverick standoff: two Association gunmen (Hired Gun) and the tally man behind them; grange riders (use Rustler for a few young hotheads) opposite; no one should die over a calf
The ambush: Jubal Stroud (Fast Gun, using his Buffalo rifle at range) and two Association gunmen (Hired Gun) on a ridge at 300 yards in failing light; they withdraw if pressed

acts.title: The Survey and the Storm
acts.description: 12 to 15 May. The railroad survey party arrives, and its records crack the mystery open: the payroll book proves the relinquishment forged, and the profile shows what the Narrows is worth. Meanwhile Ira Pettit is drinking himself toward a confession, and Henley is watching him. On the 15th the tail of a late blizzard comes down the valley and the roundup turns into a fight to hold the herd; in the howling dark, Henley takes Pettit out to the herd to kill him. This act's set piece is the storm and the stampede.
objectives: Visit the survey camp, and learn what Owen knew about the Narrows
Get the payroll book's evidence that Owen could not have signed the relinquishment
Get Ira Pettit's confession, or at least keep him alive
Hold the herd, and survive the blizzard's tail and the stampede

scenes.name: The Instrument Man
scenes.description: The survey camp. Horace Wendt is a gruff, kindly old engineer from Pennsylvania who has located three railroads and buried men on all of them. He liked Owen. He will talk to anyone who is not a Company man, and to Company men who are polite. Henry Lau, his instrument man, knew Owen better: they spent the winter in the same tent. Wendt shows the profile and the payroll book to people he trusts; Henry will show them to people Henry trusts. If the party asks the right question, how could Owen have relinquished his claim in Gilead on 10 April, the payroll book answers it: he was here, forty miles away, chaining line, every day that week. Wendt also has Owen's last letter, and the Omaha letter naming Sayre.
scenes.readAloud: The survey camp is four white wall tents in a row, as neat as soldiers, a cook tent with a stovepipe, a wagon piled with red-painted stakes, and in front of the biggest tent, on a three-legged stand, a brass instrument shining in the sun. A young Chinese man in a canvas coat and a wide hat has his eye to it, and is calling numbers to a man a quarter mile off holding a striped pole. In the tent behind him, at a drawing table covered with long rolls of paper held down by rocks, an old man with a white walrus moustache and ink to the elbows looks up at you over his spectacles. 'If you're from the Company,' he says, 'the answer is no, I won't tell you where the line goes. If you're from anyone else, there's coffee.'

skillChecks.success: Wendt unrolls the profile: grades, curves, and at the Narrows a dam, a water tank, a roundhouse and 'Div. Pt.' (CLUE E1). He opens the paymaster's box and shows you the time book: O. Lasker, chainman, foothill camp, 6 to 13 April, every day (CLUE C2). 'Relinquished in Gilead on the tenth? He was holding the far end of my chain on the tenth. I'll swear to it before any judge in the territory.'
skillChecks.failure: Wendt is polite and busy and will not open his papers for strangers. Henry Lau, walking you back to your horses, says quietly, 'Owen was my friend. Come back tonight.'

skillChecks.success: Reading Wendt's letters with him: one from the land department in Omaha asks his opinion of the Narrows site, 'offered by a local party, Mr. G. Sayre, U.S. Commissioner, title to be clear by June'. Dated 26 March. Three weeks before Owen died, Sayre was offering to sell a claim that was not his.
skillChecks.failure: Papers and more papers. You find Owen's letter to Wendt, asking that the dam leave water for the ditches below (CLUE E2), but nothing else jumps out.

skillChecks.success: Looking at the profile with a homesteader's eye: a dam at the Narrows that took the whole creek for the railroad's engines would dry every ditch below it; one that left a fair head of water, as Owen asked, would turn the valley into farms around a railroad town. Whoever controls the Narrows controls the creek. That is what this war is about.
skillChecks.failure: A lot of lines on paper. You can see there is a dam. You are not sure what it means for the creek.

scenes.name: Pettit
scenes.description: Ira Pettit, twenty, drinking in his bedroll by the grange wagon and watching Henley. Run this as a slow scene across two evenings. He wants to tell someone; he is afraid of Henley, of the rope, and of God. A kind approach works; a hard one makes him run to Henley. If the party gets him alone and promises him a trial, not a rope, and protection until then, he confesses (CLUES B6, C6), and he will swear to it before Judge Kittle. Then the party has a problem: keeping a confessed hangman alive in a camp full of men who would hang him, and away from the man who will kill him. Where do they put him? Gilead's jail (the sheriff, and the grange will hear)? The survey camp (Wendt will take him)? Calvin Booker's? Hidden in plain sight? And Henley is watching.
scenes.readAloud: He is sitting on his bedroll with his back against the grange wagon's wheel, away from the fire, where the light does not reach his face, and you can hear the bottle more than see it. A boy, really, with a sunburned neck and big raw hands and a cowboy's hat he has not grown into. When you sit down beside him he does not look at you. Out on the flats, the night guard is singing to the herd, some long slow hymn about the river, and he listens to it for a while. Then he says, very quietly, 'It takes so long. Did you know that? Nobody ever tells you it takes so long.' And then he looks up, past you, at the other fire, where a tall man with a lantern jaw is watching him, and grinning.

skillChecks.success: He wants to confess more than he wants to live, nearly. He is terrified of Henley. If you promise him a trial and protection, and he believes you, he will talk.
skillChecks.failure: A drunk boy saying something strange. Henley comes over, slaps him on the back, and walks him away to his bedroll.

skillChecks.success: He tells you everything: Sayre's office on the Friday night, $100 each and $200 to come, Sayre lettering the sign at his desk 'like he was writing a birthday card', the relinquishment they signed as witnesses next morning, the rope, the cow in the creek, Owen fighting, and how long it took (CLUES B6, C6). 'I'll say it to the judge. I want to say it. Just don't let them hang me from that tree.'
skillChecks.failure: He starts to talk and then stops. 'I can't. He'll kill me. He'll know.' He needs more than words: a safe place and a promise you can keep.

skillChecks.success: You get Pettit out of the camp at night without Henley seeing, to wherever you mean to keep him. Henley finds his bedroll empty in the morning and rides off toward Gilead to tell Sayre.
skillChecks.failure: Henley sees you go. He does not follow. He rides to Gilead at dawn, and comes back with orders.

scenes.name: The Blizzard's Tail
scenes.description: Saturday 15 May. The morning is warm and still and the sky in the northwest is the colour of a gun barrel. At two in the afternoon the wind turns, the temperature falls forty degrees in an hour, and a wall of snow comes down the valley. Everything changes: the roundup becomes a fight to hold three thousand cattle that want to drift before the storm into the creek and the breaks; men work in pairs because a man alone can be lost fifty yards from the wagon; and in the night, with lightning in the snow (thundersnow, which the old hands have seen once in their lives), the herd stampedes. Use weather_and_water for cold and exhaustion, and combat.json's stampede rules. This is the night Henley means to kill Pettit. If Pettit is with the party, Henley comes for him in the storm, with a lantern and a revolver, and it is a fight in a white-out where nobody can see ten feet. If Pettit is still at the grange wagon, Henley takes him out 'to help with night guard', and the GM should give the party a chance to notice: two riders leaving the fire, and only one coming back.
scenes.readAloud: It comes down the valley like a wall: you see it a mile off, a grey-white curtain from the ground to the sky swallowing the Narrows bluffs, then the survey tents, then the far edge of the herd, and then it is on you. The wind hits like a door slamming and the temperature drops so fast your breath freezes in your moustache, if you have one, and on your scarf if you do not. Snow so thick you cannot see your horse's ears. The cattle turn their tails to it and begin to drift, three thousand of them, a slow brown river moving south toward the creek and the breaks, and Tolliver's voice comes out of the white somewhere, hoarse, shouting for every man to ride. All afternoon you fight the herd. Then night comes, and the snow keeps falling, and somewhere far off in it, impossibly, there is thunder.

skillChecks.success: When the herd stampedes at the thunderclap, you ride for the lead, turn the leaders and start them milling; the stampede circles back on itself and stops. Nobody is killed. Tolliver, coming out of the snow, says 'I owe you', and means it. Company attitude +1.
skillChecks.failure: The stampede goes over a cutbank into the creek; you are thrown and must make a DEX save or take 2d6 bludgeoning damage, and in the morning forty head and a horse are dead in the creek, and maybe a man.

skillChecks.success: You keep your bearings in the white-out and find the wagons again; you also find, in the trampled snow at the herd's edge, a lantern still burning and two sets of horse tracks leading out, and one coming back.
skillChecks.failure: You are lost for an hour in the storm, and gain a level of exhaustion from the cold before you find the wagons by the cook's triangle, rung every minute all night for men like you.

skillChecks.success: In a lull in the wind, a single pistol shot, close, toward the herd's edge, where nothing should be shooting. If you ride for it now, you may be in time.
skillChecks.failure: Only the wind and the cattle. In the morning, Ira Pettit is found under the trampled snow at the herd's edge, 'killed in the stampede'; Dr. Haskell, if she sees the body, finds the bullet.

encounters: The stampede: a hazard (combat.json), three thousand head, in the dark and the snow
Elam Henley (Outlaw) in the white-out, with a lantern and an Army revolver, coming for Pettit; if cornered he fights, and if he can, he flees to Gilead and Sayre
Cold and exhaustion (weather_and_water) for anyone caught out after dark

acts.title: Fire on the Flats
acts.description: 16 to 22 May, the last week of the roundup. The war gets close. After the ambush and the storm, Nils Solberg plans to burn the Company's hay on the night of the 17th; if he does, Ballantine has the outrage he needs. Ballantine's telegram to Rawlins is on the pad at the Forks. Wade Tolliver, after the storm, the maverick fight and the stolen cattle in the cedar draw, is ready to be turned. And Jubal Stroud rides up to the party's fire one evening, alone, to see what kind of people they are, and to tell them the hanging was not his.
objectives: Stop the hay burning, or decide not to
Learn that the Company plans to raid the dead-list men when the thirty days run out
Turn Wade Tolliver, or at least earn his warning
Decide what to do with what the party now knows about Sayre

scenes.name: The Hay
scenes.description: The night of 17 May, the Company's hay camp: twelve stacks, two line riders, and Nils Solberg with four young homesteaders, lanterns and coal oil. The party can be there because they heard about it (from Margit, from Clara, from Lars Engstrom, or because Sayre's suggestion was overheard), or because they are guarding the hay for the Company. It is a scene with no good side: Nils is grieving and wronged and about to do something that will get people killed, and the line riders are cowboys who have done nothing. If the hay burns, the Company has its justification and in the coming winter six hundred cattle starve. If the party stops Nils, he hates them for a while; if they stop him without bloodshed, he may come to thank them.
scenes.readAloud: The hay camp is twelve long dark shapes against the stars, each as big as a house, and a line cabin with a lit window, and the creek talking in the willows. Down in the willows, five young men are crouched with their horses' reins in their hands and a can of coal oil between them, and one of them, a tall fair young man with a face streaked with dried tears and dust, is unscrewing the cap. 'Owen's dead,' Nils Solberg says to the others, low. 'Joe's shot. Their hay's the one thing they can't buy in February. Mr. Sayre said so.' He looks up at the stacks. 'Let them starve a little.'

skillChecks.success: Nils stops. If you tell him who suggested the hay and what the payroll book shows, he understands, all at once, that Sayre has been steering him all along, and he puts the can down. He will ride with you now, and he will not forget who his secretary is.
skillChecks.failure: He will not listen to strangers. The cap comes off the can. You will have to stop him by force, or watch.

skillChecks.success: You get between the young men and the stacks without being seen, and take the coal oil, or the matches, or their horses. When they find out, it is too late and too funny to fight about. Nobody is hurt.
skillChecks.failure: The line riders hear something, come out with a rifle and a lantern, and somebody on one side or the other fires at the light.

skillChecks.success: You stand up in the willows with your gun out and tell them to go home. They are boys; they go. Nils does not speak to you for a week.
skillChecks.failure: One of the boys draws. Now it is a fight between people who should be on the same side, with lit lanterns in a field of hay.

scenes.name: A Visit From Mr. Stroud
scenes.description: One evening after the storm, Jubal Stroud rides up to the party's fire alone, sits his grey horse at the edge of the light, and asks if he may share their coffee. He is curious about them: they are the people the town talks about. He is courteous, dry, and, if pressed about the hanging, coldly insulted (CLUE A5): he has never used a sign or a rope, the paper was Land Office paper, 'and I can't write like that, I never had the schooling'. He will say plainly that the thirty days for Booker, Solberg, Mallory and the rest run out on the 24th, that he will come with paper, and that anyone standing with them will be treated as one of them. He will also say, if asked why he stopped his man shooting Pruneda, 'His days weren't up. I'm not a murderer. I'm a range detective.' The scene is a portrait of a man with a code that makes him worse, not better. He leaves before the coffee is finished.
scenes.readAloud: The grey horse comes into the edge of the firelight at a walk, and stops, and its rider sits it with his hands folded on the horn, where you can see them. 'Evening,' says Jubal Stroud. 'I'd take a cup of that coffee if it's going. I've been wanting a look at you people.' He gets down without waiting for an answer, loosens his cinch, squats by the fire on his heels like a cowhand, and holds out a tin cup. In the firelight his face is long and clean-shaven and lined, and quite pleasant, and his eyes do not stop moving. 'They tell me you think I hanged Owen Lasker,' he says. 'I'd like to clear that up. It's a matter of professional pride.'

skillChecks.success: Every word about the hanging is true and he is furious about it in a cold, vain way: someone has used his Association's name on a piece of clerk's work and made him look like an amateur. He does not know who. He would quite like to.
skillChecks.failure: A killer explaining that he is not the killer. You cannot tell how much of it to believe.

skillChecks.success: You draw him out about the dead list: he has the Association's copy in his saddlebag, and the names on it 'came from a reliable local source, a man in a position to know who's filing on what'. He will not say who. He does not need to.
skillChecks.failure: He smiles. 'You're fishing.' He finishes his coffee and leaves.

skillChecks.success: You tell him, to his face, that if he comes for the dead-list men on the 24th he will have to come through you. He looks at you a long time and says, 'I believe you mean that. All right.' From now on he will offer you a fair fight before anything else, which may give the party a chance to choose the ground.
skillChecks.failure: He laughs, not unkindly, and says, 'Son, I've buried better.' A point of Reputation is lost if anyone else saw you blink.

scenes.name: Tolliver's Fire
scenes.description: The last night of the roundup, 22 May. Wade Tolliver sits alone by a small fire away from the wagons with a bottle he is not drinking. He has seen the cedar-draw cattle with worked brands, the tally man's orders, the ambush on Pruneda, a boy killed in the storm (or saved), and his own nephew (Hy Tolliver, if played) looking at him differently. He knows the date of the raid: Ballantine has told him the warrants will come on the 24th and the Company will ride on Solberg's Bend at dawn on the 26th, when the dead-list men gather there. He has been ordered to bring eight riders. He does not want to. A party that has earned his respect at the roundup can turn him: he will tell them the date and plan (CLUE D4), and on the morning of the raid, what he does depends on what the party asks of him and what he believes about the hanging. A party that has not earned it gets a warning and no more: 'Don't be at the Bend on Wednesday.'
scenes.readAloud: He has made a little fire of sagebrush in the lee of a cutbank half a mile from the wagons, the way a man does when he wants to think, and he is sitting on his saddle with his hat pushed back and a bottle beside him with the cork still in. He does not look round when you come up. 'Twelve years I've worked for this outfit,' Wade Tolliver says to the fire. 'Came up the trail from Texas with the first herd. I've done hard things for it. I've never done a dirty one.' He picks up the bottle, looks at it, puts it down again. 'Sit down. I'm going to tell you something, and then I'm going to have to decide whether I'm a range boss or a man.'

skillChecks.success: He tells you: the warrants come from Rawlins on the 24th for nine names; the dead-list men and their families will gather at Solberg's Bend on the 25th, because the grange thinks there is safety in numbers; Ballantine, Stroud, the eight Association gunmen and eight Company riders will surround the Bend before dawn on Wednesday 26th; the order is to take the men named 'or kill them resisting', and Ballantine has said 'fire the barns if they hole up'. 'I'll ride with them because if I don't, somebody worse leads my boys. What I do when I get there depends on what you can show me.' (CLUE D4)
skillChecks.failure: He tells you only: 'Don't be at Solberg's Bend on Wednesday morning. Tell the old woman too.' Then he gets up and walks back to the wagons.

skillChecks.success: He is not asking for absolution; he is asking for a reason. Show him proof the Company has been lied to about the hanging, the payroll book, Pettit, the sign, and he will have one.
skillChecks.failure: A hard old man in a bad mood. You cannot tell where he will land.

skillChecks.success: You read him like a hand of cards and bet everything: you tell him the whole truth about Sayre. He believes you. On the morning of the raid, Wade Tolliver's eight riders will not fire on women and children, and if the party can show Ballantine the proof in front of them, they will not fire at all.
skillChecks.failure: You overplay it. He thinks you are working him for the grange, and says so, and leaves.

encounters: Nils Solberg and four young homesteaders (Rustler) at the hay camp, and two Company line riders (Hired Gun or Drunk Cowboy): a fight between people who should not be fighting
Jubal Stroud at the fire: no fight unless the party starts one, in which case he leaves and comes back in daylight with an offer of a showdown
Optional: a visit to the Forks for the telegraph pad (Ballantine and Lyall; a Hired Gun on the door)

npcsInvolved.name: Wade Tolliver, 46
npcsInvolved.role: The Company's range boss and the roundup boss
npcsInvolved.description: Big, weathered, sheepskin coat, a Texas cowman who came up the trail in 1874; hard, fair, honest, and at the end of his rope.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To run a clean roundup and keep his men alive; to find out whether he still works for something he can be proud of. The key to stopping the raid.

npcsInvolved.name: Horace Wendt, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Chief engineer of the Sweetwater & Big Horn location survey
npcsInvolved.description: White walrus moustache, ink to the elbows, a Pennsylvanian who has located three railroads. Gruff, kind, neutral and stubborn.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To locate the best line, and to see Owen Lasker's widow treated fairly. He liked Owen.

npcsInvolved.name: Henry Lau (companion)
npcsInvolved.role: The survey's instrument man; Owen's tent-mate all winter
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see his friend's killer found, and to get the line through honestly.

npcsInvolved.name: Ira Pettit, 20
npcsInvolved.role: One of the hangmen; the confession waiting to happen
npcsInvolved.description: Freckled, raw-handed, drinking, terrified, riding for the grange's wagon because Sayre found him the work.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To confess and not be hanged. Dies on 15 May unless protected.

npcsInvolved.name: Elam Henley, 34
npcsInvolved.description: Long, lantern-jawed, grinning, a bay with a bar shoe and a new Army revolver.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep Pettit quiet, get his $200, and hold the Narrows paper until Sayre pays him off.

npcsInvolved.name: Jubal Stroud, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Lean, quiet, grey coat, ivory-handled revolver, a Buffalo rifle. A man with rules.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Fees, reputation, and his thirty-day code. Wants to know who used his name.

npcsInvolved.name: Nils Solberg, 24
npcsInvolved.role: Margit's son; on the dead list; Owen's best friend
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, fair, red-eyed, a good farmer and a bad enemy, carrying a carbine and a grief too big for him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Revenge, and to do something. Sayre has been steering him to the hay.

npcsInvolved.name: Calvin Booker (companion) and Joe Pruneda
npcsInvolved.role: A Tenth Cavalry veteran rancher on the dead list, and his Tejano rider
npcsInvolved.description: Booker: see his companion sheet. Pruneda: twenty-six, from San Antonio, the best horse-breaker on the creek, cheerful, sings constantly.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep Booker's Draw. Pruneda's shoulder is the first Company blood on the creek.

npcsInvolved.name: Lars Engstrom, 38
npcsInvolved.role: The grange's rep at the roundup
npcsInvolved.description: Big, fair-bearded, Swedish, in overalls, a temper like a stove lid.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Every calf that is a grange calf, and not one less.

npcsInvolved.name: Cyrus Ballantine and Duncan Lyall
npcsInvolved.role: The Company's manager and its clerk
npcsInvolved.description: Ballantine: cold, courteous, Edinburgh by way of Laramie. Lyall: a young Scots bookkeeper with ink-stained cuffs and a conscience he cannot afford.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Ballantine: clear the creek after the roundup. Lyall: keep his job without being hanged as an accessory.

rewards.money: Roundup wages for anyone riding for an outfit ($40 a month and found, prorated; about $20 for the two weeks). The grange pays $5 a head for every grange calf the party recovers from the maverick tally (up to $200 for the forty). The survey party pays $2 a day to anyone who guards its stakes from the Company's riders. Tolliver gives a $10 gold coin to whoever turned the stampede.
items: Horace Wendt's sworn statement, or the payroll and time book itself, showing Owen in the foothills from 6 to 13 April (CLUE C2)
A tracing of the survey profile with the Narrows marked 'Div. Pt.' (CLUE E1), from Henry Lau
Ira Pettit, alive, with his confession (CLUES B6, C6), if the party kept him alive
The torn warning card from the ridge above Booker's Draw
A copy of Ballantine's telegram (CLUE D3), if the party went to the Forks
The Association's annotated dead list (CLUE C3), if the party got into Ballantine's tin box

twists: Sayre found Henley and Pettit their work with the grange's wagon, as a kindness to 'two lads down on their luck', and the grange thanked him for it. The hangmen are riding for the dead man's friends.

Stroud stopped his own man from killing Joe Pruneda because Pruneda's thirty days had not run. Then he tore up Pruneda's card. He is a killer who believes in rules, and the hanging has offended him personally: he wants to know who used his Association's name. If the party ever shows him the sign's paper and tells him who keeps Land Office blanks, he will go and ask Sayre himself, which may be the end of Sayre, or of the evidence, depending on how it goes.

Ira Pettit, if he lives, is the campaign's best witness and its worst responsibility. Everyone on the creek who learns what he did will want him hanged at the Narrows cottonwood, and the party promised him a trial.

The cattle with worked brands in the cedar draw were stolen by the Company's own tally man and two riders on Ballantine's private instruction, to be counted against the homesteaders as 'rustled'. Ballantine will deny it; the tally man will not, if leaned on.
dmTips: The roundup is the campaign's showcase of the work of the West. Spend real time on it: the circle at dawn, the cut, the branding fires, the night guard singing to the herd. Let the pregens who know the work (Hy Tolliver, Clara Solberg, Calvin Booker) shine.
Pair Company and grange characters on the circle. The roundup is the one time the two sides work together; it is also the time they are most dangerous to each other.
The survey camp is where the mystery breaks. If the party has not thought to ask how Owen could have signed a relinquishment on 10 April, let Henry Lau say it: 'He was with me that week. Every day.'
Ira Pettit is a clock. If the party has not found him by the 15th, he dies in the storm, and the party learns about it in the morning; give them Henley's bullet in the body as the consolation clue.

Run the blizzard's tail as weather, not just colour: travel stops, men work in pairs, exhaustion from cold is real, and the stampede is a hazard with rules. A party that holds the herd earns Tolliver's debt, which is worth more than money in bk-scenario-003.
Stroud at the fire is the scene players remember. Play him dry, courteous and absolutely sure of himself. He is not a monster; he is a professional in a profession that should not exist.
Tolliver is the hinge of the next scenario. A party that turned him can stop the raid with words in bk-scenario-003; a party that did not will have to stop it with guns.

End the scenario with the Plainsman of Saturday 22 May: STORM ON THE FLATS. YOUNG RIDER KILLED IN STAMPEDE (or not), and a line about the Company's hay. Then put the date on the table: the thirty days run out on Monday the 24th.
